extracted.intended_audience: fiction and memoir writers seeking beta readers and writers who want to be beta readers
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for writers on how to find beta readers and how to be an effective beta reader — focused on manuscript-level feedback (beyond copyediting) and on using beta-reading as practice to improve craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flip the question to find beta readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Where can you find writers in your genre looking for a beta reader?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look to local writing communities you can join; look to genre organizations where you can network; look to online groups with solid reputations; look to those you know who read your genre who might have a thoughtful eye. Also consider that many others are looking for beta readers too (mutual exchanges).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use beta reading as practice to strengthen your editing and writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Donning an editorial hat is an education — the more you practice editing others' work, the stronger you will become as a writer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reading as an editor trains you to examine entry points, resolutions, pacing, and craft; it helps you understand hooks and tying up threads. Practice both on others' manuscripts and your own; network and be a creative partner to transform your own writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus beyond grammar, punctuation, and spelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Think about more than grammar, punctuation, and spelling perfection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beta reading is not only copyediting. While typos matter, prioritize story-level issues (character, plot, pacing, clarity) rather than treating the role as a proofreader or ghostwriter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance praise with critique
rubrics_metrics.description: Celebrate strengths just as much as pointing out areas needing more work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When you see an awesome line, celebrate it. When you love a character, let the writer know. If a scene evokes a strong emotional reaction (terror, swooning, fascination), applaud how it’s crafted. Positive notes are as instructive and motivating as corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide specific, helpful notes (identify confusion and weaknesses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Think about specific notes that could be helpful to the writer: where you are confused, where the story wanders, unclear motivations or twists, and slow sections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask concrete questions: Where are you confused? Where does the story seem to wander off-focus? Where is a motivation or plot twist unclear? Where does the story seem slow? Pinpointing moments and explaining why they don’t work is more useful than vague complaints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summarize plot and identify overarching theme
rubrics_metrics.description: After finishing, articulate the book’s plot in three sentences or fewer and state the overarching theme or takeaway you perceived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This snapshot helps the writer know whether their story and theme are communicating as intended; mismatches can be especially revealing and useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the writer’s perspective — give feedback you’d want to receive
rubrics_metrics.description: Think about what would be helpful to you if you were the writer receiving feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor your notes to be constructive and usable. Empathize with the author’s position and the stage of the manuscript when deciding depth and type of feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt an editor mindset, not a ghostwriter’s
rubrics_metrics.description: You are in 'editor' mode, not a 'ghostwriter' tasked with rewriting anything for the author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid rewriting passages for the author; instead, explain why something isn’t working and, where appropriate, suggest options or directions for revision rather than supplying finished prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique with kindness — avoid brutality
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tone matters: be honest and clear but respectful. Kind, constructive feedback maintains relationships and increases the likelihood the author can use your notes productively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify the hook (where you were truly engaged) and explain why
rubrics_metrics.description: Pinpoint the moment you were truly hooked in the manuscript (page 1 or later) and explain what made it work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explaining why a passage hooked you helps the author understand how to create or strengthen hooks elsewhere. Noting late hooks in early drafts is normal and informative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat beta reading as a mutual, educational exchange
rubrics_metrics.description: Beta reading can be more than a chore—it's a creative education and networking opportunity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer to help others and accept help in return. Use beta-reading exchanges, review blogs, and community participation to both find readers and improve your craft; consider budget and options (e.g., paid services exist but are optional).
